summary:
Poland's national law on entry, documents, custody and protection applies in Podlaskie Voivodeship and is set out in the national assessment. What is documented for the voivodeship itself concerns public LGBT assembly in Białystok and the local political setting around it.

The first Białystok Equality March took place on 20 July 2019 with about 1,000 participants. Far-right groups attacked the march and tried to block its route, and the event is described as Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ gathering. Białystok County, the district surrounding the city, was declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, in a voivodeship that was a stronghold of Law and Justice (PiS).

The fourth Białystok Equality March, on 28 September 2024, drew about 300 participants and was guarded by around 500 police officers. Counter-demonstrations appeared at several points along the route. After the gathering the regional police, through spokesman Tomasz Krupa, stated that no incidents had been recorded and assessed the event as safe. Far-right presence continued; the march passed without reported violence under heavy police cover.
tangentialFactors:
Attendance at Białystok's equality march fell from roughly 1,000 in 2019 to roughly 300 in 2024, while police deployment for the later event reached around 500 officers, a deployment larger than the demonstration it guarded.

The two marches frame a local contrast in how the same street is contested: a 2019 route that was physically attacked by far-right groups, and a 2024 route where far-right counter-demonstrations were present at several points but police recorded no incidents and judged the event safe.
localsOnly:
The LGBT-free zone declaration came from county-level government, covering the district around Białystok rather than the city administration, and was made in the same year as the first equality march.

Policing of the 2024 march was a regional police operation, and the force's spokesman Tomasz Krupa issued the post-event assessment that no incidents had been recorded. Far-right presence was reported at the 2024 event as well as at the 2019 one.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of Białystok County's LGBT-free zone declaration is not stated in these sources; whether it has been repealed, and by what act, is unresolved here.

No finding specific to Podlaskie Voivodeship on policing of trans individuals, gender-marker recognition, custodial conditions or healthcare access appears in these sources; those matters are addressed at national level.

The 2024 police assessment that no incidents were recorded is the force's own statement. The sources carry no independent account of how the counter-demonstrations behaved along the route.

The description of the 2019 march as the most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event in Poland rests on a single source and is given here without injury or arrest figures, which the sources do not supply.
